claims.text: The starting nanoparticles are near-equiatomic HEAs in a single-phase, random cation-disordered state.
Reducing oxygen partial pressure during high-temperature treatment preserves the nanoparticles' solid-solution structure.
Selective oxidation of more reactive metal constituents destabilizes the homogeneous solid solution.
Oxygen partial pressure is the only variable changed between the reduced-oxygen and ambient-oxygen treatments.
The proposed effect applies under catalytic operation at 773–1173 K.
The proposed effect applies under thermoelectric operation at 473–1923 K.
Oxygen chemical potential can be changed by controlling temperature and oxygen partial pressure.
Lower oxygen partial pressure decreases oxygen chemical potential.
Lower oxygen chemical potential retards oxidation of the more reactive metal species in the nanoparticles.
Low-oxygen conditions suppress formation of separate oxide phases.
Suppressing heterogeneous oxide formation prevents disruption of the uniformly mixed alloy solid solution.
Reduced-oxygen treatment will yield greater retention of the homogeneous near-equiatomic phase than ambient-oxygen treatment.
Reduced-oxygen treatment will yield fewer segregated oxide phases than ambient-oxygen treatment.
Reduced-oxygen treatment will improve catalytic activity or thermoelectric efficiency relative to ambient-oxygen treatment.
Under ambient oxygen, reactive alloy constituents will partially oxidize and cause phase segregation or formation of less-stable oxide phases.
The effect may weaken when oxygen is too scarce to maintain necessary oxide-sublattice buffering.
At sufficiently high temperature, oxygen partial pressure may cease to be the primary factor governing stability.
Oxygen chemical potential influences the phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing oxides, and low oxygen partial pressure may permit pure rocksalt HEO formation.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as a metallic HEA solid solution, but the mediator is described as an oxygen sublattice without explaining that such a sublattice exists in the initial alloy or is confined to a surface oxide.

The mechanism treats oxide formation as destabilizing and seeks to suppress it, whereas the boundary invokes a necessary oxide-sublattice buffering function at finite oxygen pressure; the beneficial oxide state and its relation to the metallic solid solution are not reconciled.
